subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Early March: Nandita noticed that Chinmay no longer reached for her hand on the walk back from the vegetable market. He walked half a step ahead, answering work messages. She told herself he was busy.
April: They ate dinner at the same table, each with a phone. He hadn't asked about her new team lead, the one who had made her cry in the lift. She hadn't brought it up. The evenings split on their own: his series in the bedroom, her books on the sofa.
May, a Sunday: A college friend visited and asked, "How are things with Chinmay?"
"Good," Nandita said.
After the friend left, she sat on the balcony and realised she felt lonelier in this flat than she had ever felt living alone in the hostel. She opened her mouth to call to him. Then she thought of the long, tiring conversation it would start, and closed it.

qa.q: What did Chinmay no longer do on the walk back from the market?
qa.a: Chinmay no longer reached for Nandita's hand.

qa.q: What did Nandita realise on the balcony in May?
qa.a: Nandita realised she felt lonelier in the flat with Chinmay than she had ever felt living alone in the hostel.

qa.q: What could Nandita try instead of closing her mouth?
qa.a: Nandita could start small, telling Chinmay she misses their walks and talks, rather than waiting for the right moment for a big conversation.

qa.q: How might Chinmay be experiencing these months?
qa.a: Chinmay may think things are fine, just busy, and not notice how far apart their evenings have drifted or how alone Nandita feels.

grounding: Shows a woman noticing fewer touches, less curiosity and separate evenings, feeling lonely inside the relationship yet staying silent to avoid a hard talk.

passage:
Nikita, beta, your Tanuja masi will tell you something she's never told anyone. When I was twenty-five, two years married, your uncle and I stopped holding hands. Not after a fight. It just stopped.
He came home, ate, watched the news. I came home, cooked, read. He didn't ask about my school, the children I taught, the head who shouted at me. I didn't ask about his shop. We slept in the same bed like two passengers on a night bus.
I have never been so lonely, beta. Not before marriage, not after your grandmother died. Lonely with a man sitting one metre away.
And I said nothing for almost a year. I was afraid that if I opened my mouth, a big, ugly talk would come out, and I didn't have the strength for it.
So when you say "everything's fine" in that small voice, I hear myself.

qa.q: How long did Tanuja say nothing?
qa.a: Tanuja said nothing for almost a year.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja stay silent despite feeling so lonely?
qa.a: Tanuja was afraid a big, ugly talk would come out and didn't feel strong enough for it.

qa.q: What might Tanuja's story help Nikita do?
qa.a: It might help Nikita notice the same quiet distance and speak up sooner, instead of saying 'everything's fine' in a small voice.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's husband have seen those years?
qa.a: He may have thought their life was calm and normal, not realising his wife felt lonely beside him every night.

grounding: Illustrates, in an aunt's memory, a wife feeling lonely inside her marriage as touch and curiosity faded, and saying nothing to avoid a hard talk.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
In their apartment in Buenos Aires, Valentina started keeping count without meaning to.

Jin used to kiss the back of her neck when he passed the stove. Now he said "smells good" from the doorway. He used to ask about the difficult client at her studio; now he said "how was work?" and nodded at whatever she answered. After dinner he took his laptop to the balcony, and she sat with a book on the sofa, reading the same paragraph.

Separate evenings. Every evening.

She had lived alone for years before him and had never felt this lonely. Alone, at least, no one was sitting ten feet away.

On Thursday she almost said it: "Jin, are we okay?" She got as far as his name. He looked up. She said, "Nothing. Do you want tea?"

He said yes. She made it. The question stayed in her throat.

qa.q: Where did Jin take his laptop after dinner?
qa.a: To the balcony.

qa.q: Why does Valentina feel lonelier now than when she lived alone?
qa.a: She feels lonely and unseen inside the relationship, because Jin is close by but no longer curious about her or affectionate.

qa.q: What could Valentina try instead of offering tea?
qa.a: She could gently say what she has noticed, fewer touches and separate evenings, and ask Jin how he feels, even though it is hard.

qa.q: What might Jin be experiencing when he looks up at his name?
qa.a: He may sense something is coming and feel uneasy, or he may be absorbed in his own worries and not notice the distance at all.

grounding: Valentina notices fewer touches, less curiosity and separate evenings with Jin, feels lonelier than when single, yet says nothing to avoid a hard talk.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
Rehana and Tanvir both worked at the same hospital in Lucknow, she in paediatrics, he in radiology, and for three years they had eaten lunch together in the staff canteen every day they could.

These days Tanvir ate at his desk. "Backlog," he said.

At home he was polite, even kind. But he no longer asked about the children on her ward, whose names he used to know. When she came to bed, he was already asleep, or pretending to be. On Sunday he went cycling alone.

On Tuesday Rehana saw him in the canteen after all, laughing with two colleagues over chai. He waved at her. She waved back and sat at a different table.

She was surrounded by people all day. She had never felt so alone.

That night she opened her mouth to say something, then closed it. A hard conversation felt worse than the loneliness. For now.

qa.q: Where had Rehana and Tanvir eaten lunch together for three years?
qa.a: In the staff canteen of the hospital.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she sat at a different table?
qa.a: She felt hurt and lonely, seeing Tanvir laughing with colleagues when he claimed to be too busy to eat with her.

qa.q: What small step could Rehana take at this stage?
qa.a: She could tell Tanvir calmly that she misses their lunches and his questions about her ward, and ask what has changed.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see his lunches at his desk?
qa.a: He may think of them as simply busy days, not noticing how much distance they create for Rehana.

grounding: Rehana notices Tanvir's fewer touches, less curiosity and separate time, feels lonely within the relationship, and stays silent to avoid a hard talk.

passage:
Dear Tultul,

You asked why I sounded strange on the phone. I'll tell you, but please don't tell Ma.

Mridul and I are fine. That's the problem. We're fine the way flatmates are fine.

He doesn't hold my hand on walks anymore. He doesn't ask about my research. Last week I got my paper accepted, and I told him, and he said, "Oh, nice," and went back to his phone. The old Mridul would have taken me out for kathi rolls.

We spend evenings in different rooms. I watch films on my laptop; he plays games with his friends online.

The strange thing is, when I lived in the hostel alone, I never felt this lonely. It's worse with someone right there.

I know I should talk to him. I keep waiting for the right day. It never feels like the right day.

Your didi,
Vidya

qa.q: What news did Vidya tell Mridul last week?
qa.a: That her paper was accepted.

qa.q: How does Vidya feel living with Mridul now?
qa.a: She feels lonelier than when she lived alone in the hostel, hurt by his lack of curiosity and affection.

qa.q: What would you advise Vidya about the "right day"?
qa.a: That there may never be a perfect day; a calm, kind conversation soon is better than waiting while the distance grows.

qa.q: How might Tultul feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Tultul may feel worried and protective of Vidya, and glad to be trusted with it.

grounding: Vidya's letter to her younger sister shows her noticing fewer touches, less curiosity and separate evenings, feeling lonely inside the relationship yet saying nothing.

passage: Ira, you know me, Minakshi who never stops talking, so it's strange that I can't say this at home. Siddharth and I still eat dinner together, mostly. But he eats with his laptop open, and I eat with my phone. He used to rub my feet while we watched something; I can't remember the last time. Yesterday I got a new haircut, quite short, and he said, "Oh, nice," without really looking up. Evenings, he's in the study with his headphones and I'm in the bedroom with a book I'm not reading. The strange part is, when I lived alone in Chennai I was never this lonely. Lonely with someone in the next room is a different kind. And I keep not saying it, because saying it means a big talk, and what if the big talk goes badly? So I just say, "Night," and he says, "Night," and the lights go off.

qa.q: Why does Minakshi keep not saying anything to Siddharth?

qa.a: Minakshi could choose a calm moment and say one honest sentence, such as missing their evenings together, instead of waiting for a perfect big talk.

qa.q: What might Siddharth be experiencing in these separate evenings?
qa.a: Siddharth may not have noticed how far apart they have drifted, or may feel the same distance and be avoiding it behind the laptop and headphones.
